newsitem.title: USA: Hebron deal gives leeway to new Clinton team.
newsitem.headline: Hebron deal gives leeway to new Clinton team.

text.p: Wednesday's Hebron agreement between Israel and the Palestinians gives valuable breathing space to the new Clinton administration as it prepares to face other pressing foreign policy challenges in the year ahead.

The hard-won deal could scarcely have come at a better time for Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright, who takes office next week if, as seems virtually certain, she is confirmed by the Senate.

It spares her the need to devote her attention immediately to a bothersome dispute in an area of the world where she has little direct experience -- something she would have had to do if the U.S.-mediated negotiations had failed.

Following the accord, whereby Israel will withdraw from most of Hebron immediately and complete three more pullbacks in the West Bank in 18 months, future negotiations can be left more to the parties with less need for a prominent U.S. role.

That leaves Albright free to concentrate on such issues as NATO expansion, due to be launched at a July summit, the impact that will have on ties with Russia, and, perhaps most vital of all in the long term, managing relations with China.
U.S. officials say Albright is considering making a round-the-world inaugural trip in mid-February that would focus mainly on Europe and Asia.

Day-to-day management of Middle East affairs can be left for the time being to special envoy Dennis Ross, whose success in brokering the Hebron deal follows a year of setbacks. Ross has been asked to stay on by President Bill Clinton and Albright.

But no analysts are predicting the Middle East peace process will run smoothly from now on. Outgoing Secretary of State Warren Christopher remarked with characteristic understatement Tuesday that "there will be bumps in the road".

The Hebron agreement "certainly seems to take the heat off the administration, but it may not seem that way a year from now," said David Baldwin, a foreign policy analyst at Columbia University in New York.
If there are fresh acts of violence in the region by Arabs or Jews, "both parties may turn to the U.S. and say: 'You're a party to this agreement, what are you going to do about this'," Baldwin said.

A bruising tussle looks likely over the amount of West Bank land that Israel will actually vacate, something the Hebron accord and the 1993 and 1995 Israeli-Palestinian agreements that preceded it failed to spell out.
Beyond that, a series of intractable problems looms -- borders, Palestinian refugees, Jewish settlements, Jerusalem -- in the so-called "final status" negotiations that are due to conclude by 1999.
Some diplomats and analysts think these issues, especially Jerusalem with the powerful emotions it arouses among both Jews and Arabs, will be next to impossible to resolve.

"If there is no good faith, mutual trust, no proof that (the Palestinians) are complying with signed agreements, then I really can't see how we'll be able to make progress on such dramatic issues which entail historical compromises," Israel's ambassador to Washington, Eliahu Ben Elissar, said this week.

The Palestinians and other Arabs have raised similar concerns about the good faith of Israel's right-wing Likud government, which has refused to endorse the concept of "land-for-peace" embraced by its Labour predecessor.

Despite the "powerful logic" Christopher said Wednesday he saw in the peace process, sooner or later Washington is likely again to have to go beyond its preferred role of honest broker and lean heavily on the parties to keep the process going.

In the broader Middle East context, Albright will need to decide how to tackle the fraying relations between Israel and the Arab states that has brought the slow normalisation process close to a standstill.

In particular, an Israeli-Syria peace deal that seemed within reach a year ago now looks a distant prospect following Likud's refusal to hand back the Golan Heights to Syria as Labour was prepared to do.

While Washington continues to call for a "comprehensive" peace embracing Syria and Lebanon, U.S. officials say Albright will be reluctant to repeat the experience of Christopher, whose 20-odd trips to Damascus failed to produce an accord.
